subject: Clarify SLA commitments for streaming vs. sync endpoints — token velocity expectations
messages:
From: Dana Liu <dana.liu@acmefin.com>
To: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
Cc: Jared Park <jared.park@acmefin.com>
Date: 2027-02-14T09:12:00-08:00
Subject: SLA questions on streaming vs synchronous endpoints

Hi Karthik —

Thanks for the draft SLA and the bandwidth numbers. Two items our infra team flagged while we reviewed the doc:

1) Time-to-first-token (TTFT): The SLA language ties TTFT to a per-request 95th percentile but doesn't separate streaming and synchronous endpoints. For our use case (real-time customer chat routed to underwriting rules), we need deterministic TTFT guarantees for streaming so experience on the web client is not degraded.

2) Token velocity (tokens/sec): The doc lists a sustained token/sec number but our workload includes many short-lived, high-parallelism streams (hundreds of concurrent user sessions). We need clarity on whether the sustained rate applies per-request, per-connection, or per-reservation.

Can you confirm whether Redwood would be willing to:
- Add a carve-out in Section 4.1 to specify separate TTFT commitments for streaming endpoints (e.g., 95th percentile TTFT <= 350ms for payloads <= 128 tokens) and
- Define token/sec commitments per active stream vs per-GPU-reservation and provide guidance on expected throttling behavior when concurrent streams spike?

We have a pilot in March and this clarity is a gating factor for procurement. I've attached our sample trace and the SLA draft with inline notes.

Appreciate any quick clarification so we can get legal moving.

Best,
Dana Liu
Director, Platform Engineering
Acme Financial

Attachments: acme_sla_questions.txt (notes), sample_stream_trace_20270213.json.gz
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
To: Dana Liu <dana.liu@acmefin.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-02-14T10:05:00-08:00
Subject: Re: SLA questions on streaming vs synchronous endpoints

Dana —

Thanks for the clear notes and the trace. Short answers up front: yes, we can separate TTFT by endpoint type and we can call out per-stream expectations, but the final commitments depend on the deployment option (hosted API vs Dedicated reservation) and the traffic shape. A few clarifying points so we can propose concrete wording:

- Is the client expecting streaming responses with tokenized chunks of <= 16 tokens per chunk, or larger chunk sizes? That impacts how we measure TTFT (first token vs first chunk).
- For your concurrent session counts, are the streams long-lived (minutes) or short (sub-10s queries)?
- Are you planning to use our hosted tier for pilot or request a Dedicated reservation?

I'll loop in Marissa for procurement language and Aditya for runtime/engineering guidance. If you can answer the bullets above, we'll produce a redline of Section 4 with recommended numeric thresholds and an accompanying operational note (what we monitor, what triggers throttling, and fallback behavior).

Karthik
Head of Enterprise Sales — Redwood Inference

[Sent from my laptop]
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Dana Liu <dana.liu@acmefin.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>, Legal <legal@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-02-14T11:20:00-08:00
Subject: Re: SLA questions on streaming vs synchronous endpoints

Hi Dana —

Appreciate the pilot timing context. Procurement note: we can provide explicit carve-outs in the SLA but we need to scope them to one of three profiles: Hosted Standard, Dedicated Reserved, or Private (VPC). The carve-out will include:

- TTFT commitment for streaming endpoints (95th pct)
- Sustained token/sec allowance per active stream (95th pct) and a soft burst headroom for short spikes
- Clear throttling semantics: what we do (queue, shed requests, fallback to sync model) once limits are hit

For Hosted Standard pilots we typically offer conservative per-stream commitments (e.g., 95th TTFT <= 450ms for <=128 token responses) and recommend Dedicated for production if they need sub-350ms deterministic TTFT at scale. If you are evaluating Dedicated we can include minimum reservation sizes to guarantee per-stream velocity.

I'll prepare a short redline for Section 4 and a one-page Appendix with operational examples (concurrent streams vs reservation sizing).

Marissa Cole
Sr. Manager, Enterprise Contracts
Redwood Inference

Attachment: acme_sla_draft_v2.pdf (redline to follow)
From: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>
To: Dana Liu <dana.liu@acmefin.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-02-14T14:38:00-08:00
Subject: Re: SLA questions on streaming vs synchronous endpoints

Thanks all — adding some engineering context so the carve-outs map to measurable signals. Notes below are intended to be translated verbatim into Appendix A (operational behavior):

1) TTFT measurement
- For streaming endpoints we measure TTFT as the time from request accepted to first byte framed to the client (first token delimiter). If you stream in multi-token chunks we record the time of the first byte of the chunk.
- We report 95th percentile TTFT over a rolling 24-hour window per-customer per-endpoint. SLA breach triggers are per-reservation (for Dedicated) and per-customer (for Hosted).

2) Token velocity semantics
- We define two related metrics: per-active-stream sustained throughput (tokens/sec at 95th pct over a 5-minute sliding window) and per-reservation aggregate throughput (tokens/sec across all streams tied to a reservation).
- For Hosted Standard: we provision per-request shaping, so per-active-stream expected sustained throughput is conservative (default 10-15 tokens/sec for typical chat payloads). Burst headroom is modeled as short 30s windows where token/sec can spike up to 4x but is not guaranteed beyond that.
- For Dedicated reservations: we can guarantee higher per-stream sustained rates (e.g., 25+ tokens/sec) and explicit aggregate capacity based on reserved GPU compute. Reservation sizing guidance: N concurrent medium streams (<= 128 tokens) per GPU = ~X (we'll run a small calibration during pilot).

3) Failure/fallback behavior
- When an endpoint exceeds per-stream limits we prefer queuing up to a configurable latency bound (default 500ms) before shedding and returning an explicit 429 with a retry-after header. For mission-critical customers we can change that to graceful fallback to a smaller model instance or to a sync endpoint with documented behavior.

4) Monitoring and evidence
- We will publish token-level telemetry in the Console (per-route plots) and provide a sample trace (attached). For contractual evidence we can provide daily aggregated reports and, for Dedicated customers, a shared Prometheus endpoint for the reservation.

Action items from engineering:
- Karthik/Marissa: confirm whether you want numbers drafted for Hosted Pilot or Dedicated baseline.
- Dana: confirm chunk size and expected session duration distribution (short queries vs long sessions).

I'll draft Appendix A and hand to Marissa for inclusion in the SLA redline.

— Aditya
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: SLA questions on streaming vs synchronous endpoints

Karthik/Marissa/Aditya —

Thanks — that level of detail helps a lot. Quick answers:
- Chunking: client will emit small chunks (8–16 tokens typical) to reduce perceived latency.
- Session distribution: ~70% short queries (1–6s), 30% long sessions (2–8 minutes) for underwriting chat. Peak concurrent active streams expected ~420 for pilot, with burst to ~1.2k for seasonal spikes.
- Pilot will run on Hosted initially; we'll evaluate Dedicated for production if the numbers require deterministic TTFT < 350ms.

Please proceed with a redline for Hosted Pilot numbers and an Appendix that shows how a Dedicated reservation would change the guarantees. If we can get that by Monday (2027-02-16) we can keep procurement on track.

Dana
Director, Platform Engineering
Acme Financial
